q: A JD says 'own the RAG platform, optimise latency and cost, partner with security'. Which prep focus is best aligned?
options: Ingestion, caching, latency/cost design and IAM/security trade-offs
why: The responsibilities are platform ownership, performance and security, so design rounds will cover those. Prompt tricks alone are the best distractor but do not cover platform concerns.

q: A RAG app gives wrong answers and a peer suggests a bigger model. What is the best first step?
options: Check whether retrieval returns the right passages on an eval set
why: Most failures originate in retrieval or data; measuring recall first isolates the stage. A bigger model cannot use passages that were never retrieved.

q: Self-hosting an LLM makes the most economic sense when:
options: Volume is high and steady so GPUs stay well utilised
You need the highest frontier quality on hard tasks
why: Self-hosting cost is dominated by GPU utilisation; steady high load amortises it. Low or spiky traffic leaves GPUs idle, making the API cheaper.

q: Which statement best separates an AI Engineer from a GenAI Data Scientist?
options: The AI Engineer owns the running LLM service; the GenAI DS owns experiment and evaluation evidence
The AI Engineer only writes prompts
The GenAI DS owns on-call and deployment
why: Engineers are accountable for production reliability, cost and latency; DS roles for experiments and metrics. Both care about eval, so they overlap but differ in ownership.

q: An interviewer gives a one-line prompt: 'Design an AI assistant for our company'. What is the best first move?
options: Draw a multi-agent architecture with a vector database
Ask targeted questions on scale, data, quality bar and constraints, then state assumptions
Pick the strongest available model and describe prompts
Ask for the full requirements document before saying anything
why: Stated assumptions anchor the design and let the interviewer correct you early. Jumping to architecture ignores requirements; waiting for a full spec is unrealistic.

q: Requirement: Q&A over one 20-page policy for 15 users. Which design is most defensible?
options: Place the document in context with prompt caching and cite sections
Fine-tune a model on the policy
Agent with five tools and a vector DB
why: Small stable corpus fits in context; caching reduces cost. The others add components no requirement forces.

q: Your semantic cache returns wrong-product answers. Which fix is best?
options: Include product/locale metadata in the key and tighten the threshold
why: Metadata in the key prevents cross-context hits and a stricter threshold reduces false matches. Loosening threshold worsens it.

q: Which statement about agents versus workflows is the sound design position?
options: Agents remove the need for evals
Use workflows when steps are known; agents only for open-ended paths, with step and budget limits
why: Workflows are cheaper and more predictable; agents add capability but also loops, cost and risk.

q: A support bot prompt says 'only show the current user's data' yet leaks other customers' data. What is the right fix?
options: Strengthen the wording of the prompt
Scope tool and retrieval queries to the authenticated user server-side
why: Authorisation must be enforced in code; prompts are not a security boundary, so wording and temperature cannot guarantee isolation.

q: Latency and error rates are stable after a deploy, but users complain about worse answers. What best detects this?
options: Traces with prompt/model versions plus sampled online eval scores
why: Quality regressions are silent; versioned traces and eval scores reveal them, while infrastructure metrics do not.

q: Which is the strongest trade-off statement?
options: We use Pinecone because it is popular
Vector DBs are always better than Postgres
A semantic cache cuts cost but risks wrong hits; for FAQs I accept it with a strict threshold, for account queries I skip it
why: It names gain, cost, the deciding requirement and a scoped decision, instead of naming a tool or claiming universality.

q: A bank forbids customer data leaving its network. Which design change follows?
options: Use a public frontier API with redaction only
Self-host or private-endpoint models and keep the index in-network, measuring quality gap with evals
Cache everything in a third-party service
why: Residency constraints push toward in-network inference; evals quantify the quality trade-off.

q: Processing millions of documents, which measure most improves reliable quality?
options: Schema validation, confidence scoring and human review of low-confidence extractions
Process each document once with no retries
why: At scale small error rates multiply; validation and review loops contain them. Larger models alone do not give guarantees.

q: A research agent's report contains citations that do not support the claims. Best mitigation?
options: Attach source IDs to notes and run a verifier that checks claims against cited passages
Ask the model to be more careful
why: Verification against source passages catches unsupported claims; instructions alone do not.

q: Users of a RAG assistant see documents they should not. What is the correct place to enforce permissions?
options: In the system prompt asking the model to hide restricted data
Filtering chunks by the user's ACLs at retrieval time, before prompt construction
Post-processing the answer to remove sensitive words
Encrypting the vector store at rest
why: Once restricted text reaches the prompt the model can leak it, so filtering must occur at retrieval. Encryption at rest protects storage, not per-user visibility.

q: Queue workers retry failed LLM calls immediately and the provider keeps returning 429. Best fix?
options: Exponential backoff with jitter, concurrency capped to the rate limit, DLQ after max attempts
why: Backoff plus a limiter reduces pressure on the provider; more workers or unlimited retries amplify the storm.

q: Why can 5,000 concurrent users be far fewer than 5,000 simultaneous LLM calls?
options: Users spend most time reading or typing; load is rate times latency
why: Little's law ties concurrency to request rate and latency; users idle between questions. Streaming helps perceived latency but not load.

q: Quality fell a week after launch with no deploys. What is the strongest first step?
options: Replay a fixed eval set and build a change timeline (ingestion, model alias, traffic mix)
why: A fixed set separates system change from query-distribution change; tuning before diagnosis may fix nothing.

q: In a failing RAG answer the gold passage is not in the retrieved top-k. What does this tell you?
options: The failure is upstream of generation: chunking, embeddings, filters or search
why: The generator cannot use absent evidence, so fix retrieval first; prompt edits cannot recover missing context.

q: Your pipeline needs a fallback when the primary LLM is down. Which design is best?
options: Timeout, brief retry, secondary model, cache, search-only results, then honest error, behind a circuit breaker
why: A tested degradation ladder preserves service; endless retries cause cascading failure.

q: A key leaks in a repo. Which is correct?
options: Revoke and rotate immediately, review usage, add secret scanning
why: Git history and forks keep the key, so revocation is required; deletion alone leaves it valid.

q: An agent keeps repeating an identical failing search. Which combination best addresses it?
options: Repeat-call detection plus actionable tool errors plus explicit give-up rule
why: Detection and clearer errors change the agent's behaviour; a larger window only lets it loop longer.

q: Invoice field extraction with fixed steps is handled by an agent that is slow and inconsistent. Best design?
options: A deterministic workflow with schema-constrained extraction and validation
A larger model with more tools
why: The path is known, so a workflow is cheaper and testable; agents suit unpredictable paths.

q: An email-reading agent can also send mail to any address. What is the main risk and fix?
options: Prompt-injected exfiltration; allow-list recipients and require approval for sends
why: Untrusted content plus an outbound channel enables data exfiltration; controls belong in the tool layer, not the prompt.

q: Why are pass rates over many trials preferred to one successful run?
options: Trajectories vary with sampling, so one success may be luck
why: Variance compounds along the path, so reliability must be estimated statistically.

q: Agent cost per task is much higher than expected. Which explains it best?
options: Context resent each step grows with large tool outputs and many steps
why: Each step resends accumulated context, so large tool outputs multiply input tokens.

q: In a failing trajectory the final answer is wrong. Where do you start debugging?
options: The first step where behaviour deviated from correct
why: Later steps typically follow from earlier errors; fixing the first fault removes downstream symptoms.

q: Reviewers approve 99% of agent requests within seconds. Best interpretation?
options: Possible rubber-stamping or over-gating; tier by risk and audit samples
why: Fast blanket approval shows gates may add latency without safety; risk-tiering and audits keep checkpoints meaningful.

q: A new model is announced with big benchmark gains. What is the best first step?
options: Run it on your own eval set under identical prompts and measure cost and latency
Judge it from the vendor demo
why: Own-task evals predict your outcome; benchmarks and demos may not transfer. Waiting or migrating blindly skips evidence.

q: Which is the strongest sign of a real capability change?
options: A task that failed reliably on your eval now passes consistently, or cost drops enough to unlock new use cases
why: Observable changes on your own hard cases or a large cost shift are evidence; popularity and branding are not.

q: You swapped the model and rewrote the prompt in the same release, and quality dropped. What is the main lesson?
options: Change one variable at a time so effects can be attributed
why: Changing both prevents attribution. Isolate model effects first, then tune prompts.

q: Which rollout sequence is the most sound?
options: Offline eval gate, shadow traffic, small canary, gradual expansion with rollback rules
why: Each stage catches different failures and rollback criteria keep risk bounded.

q: Best structure for 'How do you stay current?'
options: I read everything on social media
Few trusted sources, a regular rhythm, hands-on tests via my eval process, and a concrete outcome
why: It shows filtering and applied learning; volume without outcome does not demonstrate judgement.

q: Which project is best to defend in depth?
options: The one using the newest framework
One where you owned decisions, faced constraints and can quantify the result
A tutorial clone with a polished UI
A team project where your role was small
why: Depth and ownership let you survive probing; novelty and polish do not.

q: An interviewer asks 'why not RAG?' for a 30-page rarely changing manual assistant. Best answer?
options: The manual fits in context with prompt caching, avoiding retrieval misses; I would add RAG when size or update rate grows
why: It reasons from requirements and gives a revisit threshold, unlike dismissal or ignorance.

q: Which is the best reason to fine-tune?
options: Make a small model match a larger one on a high-volume narrow task, proven on your eval
why: Fine-tuning shapes behaviour and cost-efficiency; changing facts belong in retrieval and evals are still required.

q: What best justifies using an agent?
options: The path depends on intermediate results and measurements show gains over a fixed workflow
why: Autonomy has cost and risk, so evidence of benefit over a workflow baseline is needed.

q: At 100x traffic, which issue most often breaks an LLM app before CPU limits?
why: Token throughput quotas and spend scale with traffic; mitigations are caching, routing, batching and fallback.

q: You must halve LLM cost and have no breakdown. First action?
options: Instrument cost per component and segment, then target the biggest contributor and verify with evals
why: Measurement identifies the main driver; blind cuts risk silent quality loss.

q: Which statement about quantified outcomes is strongest?
options: p95 latency fell from 6 s to 2.5 s on a 500-request load test, measured before and after streaming and caching (illustrative)
why: It has baseline, method and sample, making the claim testable.

q: Interviewer asks about a failure. Which response is best?
options: Stale index caused outdated citations; I detected it through feedback traces, added change-triggered re-indexing and a freshness monitor
why: A real failure with detection, cause, fix and prevention shows maturity.

q: Which opening makes a design answer strongest?
options: Stating 3-5 assumptions about scale, data and risk, then the simplest design
why: Assumptions frame choices and are adjustable; starting with tools or a full diagram hides reasoning.

q: The interviewer seems lost in your parameter details. Best response?
options: Return to purpose and trade-off, then ask if deeper detail is useful
why: Adjust altitude and check in; unwanted internals hide structure.

q: Which trade-off answer is best for 'RAG or long context'?
options: For a small stable corpus use long context with caching; switch to RAG when size, update rate or cost per query grows
why: It decides for the scenario and names a switching trigger instead of hedging.

q: You are asked a question about a technique you have not used. What is best?
options: Say you have not used it, reason from related concepts, and outline how you would test it
why: Honest uncertainty plus an empirical plan builds trust; bluffs are easily probed.

q: Thirty minutes into a design, you have not discussed evals or security. What do you do?
options: Summarise progress and cover evals, security, observability and cost briefly, asking where to go deeper
Wait for the interviewer to ask
why: Cross-cutting concerns are expected; a concise sweep recovers coverage.

q: Which behavioural answer is strongest?
options: My role, the decision I made between two chunking strategies using 150 real questions, a cut in handling time of about a third (illustrative), and the stale-content failure I fixed
We built a chatbot and it worked well
why: It shows ownership, evaluation, a result and a failure, which is the full structure.

q: A model lacks knowledge of your constantly updated internal policies. Best lever?
options: RAG over the current policy documents with citations
Longer system prompt of all policies
why: Retrieval supplies fresh facts and can cite; fine-tuned facts are lossy and stale. A static prompt cannot hold a large changing corpus.

q: Which scenario best justifies fine-tuning?
options: High-volume narrow classification where a small tuned model must match a large model's accuracy cheaply
why: Fine-tuning pays off for stable narrow tasks with enough data and volume; knowledge that changes belongs in RAG.

q: What does QLoRA do?
options: Freezes a quantized base and trains LoRA adapters in higher precision
why: The frozen quantized base saves memory while small adapters carry the learning, enabling large-model tuning on one GPU.

q: After deploying a fine-tuned model, outputs are subtly worse with no errors. What is a likely silent cause?
options: Serving uses a different chat template than training
why: A template mismatch changes the input format the model learned, degrading quality silently.

q: Offline 92%, live 80%. Replaying the offline set on the production stack still scores 92%. Conclusion?
options: Model and serving are consistent; live input distribution or labelling differs
why: Same score on the same inputs rules out skew; investigate shifted queries or how live labels are produced.

q: The accuracy drop is concentrated in long inputs. First suspect?
options: Context truncation or length mismatch between training and serving
why: Long-input-specific failure points to truncation or length limits; rank or temperature would affect all inputs.

q: Errors spike right after a deploy that changed the prompt. Best first mitigation?
options: Roll back or flag off the prompt change while investigating
why: A reversible, correlated change is the fastest safe fix; scaling and retries do not address a faulty prompt and may amplify load.

q: Latency and tokens per request rose, traffic flat. Most likely?
why: More tokens per request means longer processing; inspect retrieval size, history and prompt changes.

q: Which retry policy is safest for a rate-limited provider?
options: Backoff with jitter, Retry-After honoured, capped attempts and a retry budget
why: Spreading and limiting retries avoids retry storms; blind retries amplify the 429s.

q: Error rate and latency look normal but thumbs-down doubled. What is this?
options: A quality regression needing quality-signal investigation
why: The service is healthy but answers are worse; check model alias, retrieval, prompt and data changes.

q: Self-hosted GPU pods take minutes to start while traffic spikes. Best response?
options: Scale on queue depth early, keep warm headroom, fallback to API during warm-up
why: Slow startup requires leading signals and spare capacity; reacting late means users wait during warm-up.

q: When does self-hosting usually beat an API on cost?
options: High steady throughput with well-utilised GPUs
why: Fixed GPU cost amortises over steady load; idle GPUs make the API cheaper.

q: What is a one-line role thesis supposed to pick?
options: Builder, researcher, or platform — backed by a project
why: Pick one spine and back it with a project.

q: What belongs in the opening 90 seconds?
options: Role, strongest project, and the constraint you care about
why: Role, project, constraint — then stop.

q: When you quote a quality number in a RAG interview, what must you add?
options: The sample size (and that you measured it)
why: Only quote metrics you measured; say n.

q: Which four boxes should you be able to draw blind for RAG?
options: Ingest, retrieve, generate, eval — plus one failure
why: Ingest, retrieve, generate, eval, and one failure mark.

q: What is the RAG interview trap called out in this module?
options: Citing a title you never retrieved
Asking for a glass of water
why: Do not cite a document you did not retrieve.

q: What is the agent interview trap?
options: Calling a workflow an agent, or an agent a workflow
why: Keep the words honest. A DAG is not an agent.

q: When should you refuse to fine-tune?
options: When labels are thin or unstable, or RAG already solves freshness
why: No stable labels, or RAG already owns freshness — refuse the tune.

q: What belongs in a 60-second LoRA answer?
options: Low-rank adapters, what you freeze, and how you eval forgetting
why: Adapters, freeze, forgetting eval — that is the minute.

q: What is the skeleton of a production incident story?
options: Symptom, pin, rollback, and the eval case you added
why: Symptom, pin, rollback, new case.

q: In what order do you debug a sudden quality drop?
options: Rewrite the UI, then buy GPUs
Check pin, retrieval, prompt id, then traffic mix
why: Pin, retrieval, prompt id, traffic mix — in that order.

q: What is the system-design timebox order?
options: Requirements first, then one design, then costs and eval
Eval only if time remains after six vendors
why: Requirements, one design, costs and eval.

q: Under time pressure, what do you cut first?
options: The second agent, the graph, or the extra reranker
why: Cut extras. Do not cut grounding or eval.

q: What is a weekly reading budget that actually sticks?
options: One paper or post, one note in your own words, one thing you might try
why: One, one, one — in your own words.

q: What is the hype filter?
options: If a blog has pictures it is production-ready
If there is no eval and no failure mode, it is a demo
If a CEO tweets it, ship it
If the model is new, it is better
why: No eval and no failure mode means demo.

q: What does STAR-L add to a project story?
options: Situation, task, action, result, and what you learned — plus a real number
why: STAR plus learned, with a number you measured.

q: How do you tell a conflict story in this loop?
options: Name the teammate who was wrong
Own a trade-off you made, without a villain
Invent a villain in another company
why: A trade-off you owned, not a teammate you blamed.

q: What is the mock loop?
options: Timed answers, recorded, scored, then the two weakest dimensions next week
why: Time, record, score, repeat the weak parts.

q: What makes a strong close?
options: Generic culture prompts you could ask any company
Questions that show you understand their stack
Asking how soon you can be VP
why: Close on their stack, not generic culture.
